 The Disproportionate Impact of Climate Change on the Global South 
 Section I 
 Climate change affects all countries, but the impacts affect the Global South more. For 
 example, rising sea levels affect island nations in the south, food insecurity affects lower-income 
 countries, displacement due to weather affects the south a lot, and poverty affects the whole south. 
 While there are treaties to try to stop climate change causes like fossil fuels, many countries are not 
 meeting the goals. For example, the Paris Agreement is an agreement to limit global warming from 
 fossil fuels, and each country has goals based on its development and financial capabilities.  1 
 Rising sea levels are affecting countries that are either surrounded by ocean or have a large 
 border with the ocean. China, Bangladesh, India, Australia, and the Pacific islands are some of the 
 countries most at risk  2  . Rising sea levels cause flooding, coastal erosion, and flooding of deltas.  3 
 Flooding would affect not only human life, but also affect wildlife both on beaches, and the water. Not 
 only that, but flooding also greatly affects humans directly through property damage, health risks from 
 the water, housing displacement, and crops and livestock loss.  4  All of this places great economic strain 
 on the Global South, further driving poverty. Coastal erosion is when flooding, waves, and rising sea 
 levels slowly take away from the land. The rising sea levels take away sand, rocks, and soil to the 
 ocean, cutting down the land piece by piece.  5  Flooding of deltas is expected to happen more often due 
 to climate change, and coastal flooding, because of rising sea levels and climate change. This has a 
 great effect on wildlife and populations near rivers.  6

 Food insecurity is caused by climate change through droughts, heat waves, and heavy rainfall. 
 All the effects of the disasters caused by climate change ruin the crops, so people have less, and have 
 to put more money toward the crops. Because of this, food becomes more expensive, causing about 30 
 million people in low-income areas to experience food insecurity.  7  Food insecurity is related to 
 poverty because people that already struggle to pay for food are even further affected by poverty when 
 food insecurity becomes more intense.  8  About 1.5 billion people are multidimensionally poor, as of 
 2022, including 593 million children under 18.  9  Food insecurity causes illnesses because hungry 
 people are affected by diet-related chronic diseases more than others.  10 
 Climate change is causing the weather to be more extreme in the Global South, forcing many 
 people to leave their homes in search of safety. An average of about 21.5 million people have been 
 displaced every year, since 2008.  11  In 2023, that leads to about 322.5 million people. This causes 
 people to lose all their possessions and leads to people being unemployed in a new country. This leads 
 to poverty, and possibly hunger.  12  Looking at 2021 statistics, China had the most people displaced due 
 to disaster, with 6.04 million. India, Indonesia, and the Philippines were also greatly affected.  13  This 
 shows how largely populated countries are being affected greatly.

 Although the effects seem unstoppable, the United Nations has resolutions in place to slow 
 the effects. Not only that, but many countries are also getting involved. The most notable and known 
 agreement is arguably the Paris Agreement, by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate 
 Change (UNFCCC), an agreement that aims to stop climate change, with each country having its own 
 goals. The agreement works in 5-year intervals, with the country's goals getting more ambitious every 
 time.  14  The UNFCCC has an annual Conference of the Parties (COP) where the parties are represented 
 at a different location every year, and currently are on their 27th.  15  At each conference, the parties 
 discuss their progress toward goals for climate change and discuss how to combat climate change.  16 
 The main goals are to stop burning fossil fuels. When fossil fuels are burnt, carbon dioxide and 
 methane are both released into the atmosphere. Those molecules both trap heat, causing climate 
 change.

 not have the flexibility to aid the Global South, receiving aid themself recently.

 The Environmental Impact of the Pharmaceutical Industry 
 Worldwide, pharmaceutical companies are producing millions of medicines each day. In 
 the process of production, chemicals are released into their surrounding environment and into 
 ecosystems. These chemicals are called Environmentally Persistent Pharmaceutical Pollutants 
 (EPPPs). The residues from production make their way into rivers, lakes, and other bodies of 
 water. Not only do EPPPs come from production, but veterinary medicines are in manure, which 
 is also used as fertilizer, contaminating the soil. Human waste provides the perfect transportation 
 of EPPPs to wastewater. Overall, EPPPs are moving from different sources to new areas creating 
 a domino effect, and making their appearance almost everywhere. In these areas where EPPP 
 concentration is higher, they are producing new species of microbes that become resistant to the 
 chemicals in the medicines. This is called Anti-Microbial Resistance (AMR). AMR lowers the 
 effectiveness of the current medicines, making them no longer work. 
 Anti-Microbial Resistance has consistently been a main topic in the World Health 
 Organization for the past two decades. The World Health Assembly has adopted multiple 
 resolutions and continues to track progress because AMR is one of the largest threats to our 
 advances in medicine. In 1998, the World Health Assembly (WHA) created Resolution WHA 
 51.17: Emerging and Other Communicable Diseases: Anti-Microbial Resistance. During the 
 WHO June 2000 Geneva consultation, WHO came up with a strategy for the containment of 
 Anti-Microbial Resistance. This contains recommendations for reducing the incorrect use of

 At the 54th World Health Assembly in 2001, two AMR resolutions were established. 
 First, WHA 54.11; WHO’s medicine strategy. Resolution WHA 54.14 focused on Global Health 
 Security; Epidemic Alert and Response. 
 During the 2005 58th World Health Assembly, resolution WHA 58.27 Improvement of 
 Anti-Microbial Resistance was created. This resolution asked for support from the 
 Director-General for ample support and supply to pick up the pace on resolutions WHA 51.17 
 and WHA 54.14 on containing anti-microbial resistance. In the same year, resolution EB120.R12 
 was passed to set up a plan for the rational use of drugs worldwide. These were both a substantial 
 part of the 2007 progress report on technical and health matters, WHA A60/28. 
 By the year 2011, the AMR situation was at large. The 2011 World Health Day sponsored 
 by the World Health Organization (WHO) was themed on anti-microbial resistance (AMR) to 
 raise awareness of the issue. The World Health Organization published Options for Action; The 
 Evolving Threat of Anti-Microbial Resistance, in 2012. Alongside, a global action plan (GAP) 
 on Anti-Microbial Resistance. The Global Action Plan includes 5 main goals. (1) One Health, a 
 plan that involves multiple committees because AMR affects everyone. (2) Sanitation, in order to 
 prevent infection to lessen the need for treatment. (3) Equitable access for

 In May 2014, WHA 67.25 was published. Again, focusing on Anti-Microbial Resistance. 
 Over the years, in 2015, 2016, and 2021 multiple global action plans were created and revised 
 for AMR. Finally, in 2019, resolution WHA 72.5 was implemented, once again accelerating and 
 adding to the process of combating AMR. 
 In 2019, Latvia published a National Action Plan (NAP) available in the World Health 
 Organization’s library of anti-microbial resistance national action plans. In June of 2022, the 
 Ministry of Health Republic of Latvia published  Latvia’s  Experience on AMR Policy 
 Development.  This contains goals for the 2023-2027  period which is essentially the next set 
 target for their National Implementation Plan. The main points mentioned in the document were 
 important international documents, most importantly the  European Union (EU) One Health 
 Action Plan Against AMR  released in 2017,  the 2023-2027  AMR action plan, policy objectives, 
 and common objectives. 
 The framework of the action plan is based on the European Union’s (EU’s) One Health 
 AMR Action Plan published in 2017. The first key objective was to make the European Union 
 the best-practice region in controlling the spread of AMR. To do this, they needed the second key 
 objective which is boosting research, developing solutions and technology, and implementing of

 In the 2023-2027 action plan, Latvia’s Ministry of Health identified their unfulfilled 
 actions for 2019-2020 and moved them to the next planning period (2023-2027). The next part of 
 the action plan mentions LATOHOP- a project led by the Swedish Board of Agriculture and the 
 Public Health Agency, the project provides tools and newer ways of communication between 
 parts of Latvia to fight AMR as a country. This section of the action plan discusses the proposals 
 within the groups in LATOHOP for AMR resources and prioritizing measures. Not only are there 
 proposals from LATOHOP in the action plan, but they are also taking approaches from experts, 
 such as a proposal for the establishment of a competence center in the field of public health. 
 Section II 
 The goal of the upcoming/current action period regarding the policy was to (1) 
 Encourage controlling the spread of AMR, leaving the need for organizations and governments 
 to work together and (2) promote responsible use of antimicrobials, changing the way they are 
 currently used in human and animal health. The new objectives included monitoring the use of 
 antimicrobials in hospitals by keeping data and surveillance in order to control the spread of 
 diseases. Prevention and control are especially important for diseases such as

 Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB), which is spread through bacteria and affects the 
 lungs. 
 Not only are veterinary and human hospitals a part of controlling the spread, but so are 
 institutions. Pharmacies and other institutions involved with medicine must cooperate in 
 collecting data and slowing the spread of disease through surveillance, data keeping, and proper 
 sanitation. Funding should be more towards the creation of AMR research laboratories to gain a 
 better understanding of the antimicrobials. The Ministry of Health promotes research in 
 environmental and health areas and hopes to create a method for tracking anti-microbial 
 resistance in bodies of water where they are highly popular. Finally, to get the country working 
 together, the people must be a part of the process, not just the professionals. Education in the 
 proper use of antibiotics for the general public is extremely important because they are the 
 majority of the people using antibiotics and spreading antimicrobial resistance. 
 Section III 
 The Delegation of Latvia proposes a solution to enhance research and education for the 
 general public. Most anti-microbial-resistant bacteria grow in bodies of water such as rivers and 
 lakes. Latvia contains many rivers and small lakes including the Daugava River, Lielupe River, 
 the Gauja River, Lake Burtnieks, Lake Lubans, and Pape Lake. Using 10 million dollars funded 
 by WHO’s core voluntary contributions (CVC), at each body of water, an AMR research 
 laboratory would be constructed. To gain awareness of the general public, the l

 NGO volunteers from Alliance to Save Our Antibiotics, Health Care Without Harm Europe, and 
 Patients’ Organizations “Together With You” which are all award-winning NGOs for their 
 contributions to the AMR cause. On one day of the weekend, business dinners could be held at a 
 waterfront venue near each laboratory where the business would discuss their tasks, or whatever 
 they were there for. A few of the scientists working in the lab would be responsible for informing 
 the attendees at the dinner a little bit about the research they do, what AMR is, and what the 
 average person can do to help. If the solution is successful, similar laboratories and activities 
 involving the general public would be then implemented in countries in the EU, and possibly
